rules.text: A single expense of up to 300 AZN may be approved by the employee's line supervisor.
A single expense above 300 AZN and up to 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the department manager.
A single expense above 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the Finance Director.
Alcohol is not reimbursable under any circumstances.
An original receipt or invoice must be attached to every expense claim above 50 AZN.
Expense claims must be submitted within 30 days.
Late claims may be accepted with the consent of the department manager.
The same expense may not be claimed more than once.
Domestic business travel is permitted when it is necessary.
The department manager decides whether a trip is necessary.
Hotel accommodation is reimbursed up to 150 AZN per night.
A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
No receipts are required for the per diem.
Air travel must be booked in economy class.
An employee may request a cash advance of up to 1,000 AZN for a business trip.
The advance must be settled after the trip by submitting receipts or returning the unspent cash.
Client entertainment is reimbursed up to 100 AZN per person, with the approval of the department manager.
The employee must record the names of the clients entertained.
The Finance Department owns this policy and may update it at any time.

findings.policy_basis: Hotel accommodation is reimbursed up to 150 AZN per night.
findings.scenario: The employee books a 30‑night hotel stay and claims the full 150 AZN for each night, exploiting the lack of a total‑trip cap.
findings.fix: Hotel accommodation reimbursement is limited to 150 AZN per night and a maximum of 30 nights per business trip.
findings.reason: The rule caps reimbursement per night but does not limit total nights, allowing unlimited claim amounts.

findings.policy_basis: Hotel accommodation is reimbursed up to 150 AZN per night.
findings.scenario: The employee claims hotel reimbursement for nights when they stayed with a colleague who offered a free room, because the rule does not require the accommodation to be actually paid for.
findings.fix: Hotel accommodation reimbursement is payable only for nights for which a valid receipt or invoice showing payment is provided.
findings.reason: The rule does not require the accommodation to have been actually paid for, so free rooms can be claimed.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense above 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the Finance Director.
findings.scenario: The employee files two separate claims of 2,100 AZN and 2,050 AZN; each is individually approved by the Finance Director, allowing reimbursement of more than the intended single‑expense limit.
findings.fix: Add: "An employee may not submit more than one expense claim exceeding 2,000 AZN for the same trip or project."
findings.reason: The rule caps a single expense above 2,000 AZN but does not limit the number of separate claims, enabling multiple large reimbursements.

findings.policy_basis: An employee may request a cash advance of up to 1,000 AZN for a business trip.
findings.scenario: The employee submits three separate advance requests for 1,000 AZN each for three consecutive trips, because the rule limits only the amount per request, not the total amount an employee may receive.
findings.fix: An employee may receive a cash advance of up to 1,000 AZN per calendar month, with total advances not exceeding 1,000 AZN without additional Finance Director approval.
findings.reason: The cash‑advance rule limits only the amount per request, not the cumulative amount an employee may obtain.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense above 300 AZN and up to 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee splits a 2,500 AZN purchase into two separate expenses of 1,250 AZN each; each is a “single expense” within the 300‑2,000 AZN band and only needs the department manager’s written approval, bypassing the Finance Director.
findings.fix: Require that related expenses whose combined total exceeds 2,000 AZN receive Finance Director approval.
findings.reason: Splitting a >2,000 AZN purchase into two expenses each under 2,000 AZN avoids the Finance Director’s approval requirement.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense above 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the Finance Director.
findings.scenario: The Finance Director, who also travelled for business, signs the approval for their own 2,500 AZN expense, since the policy never forbids the claimant from being the approver.
findings.fix: Add: "The Finance Director may not approve expense claims submitted by themselves."
findings.reason: The Finance Director can approve their own 2,500 AZN expense because the policy does not require a different approver.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense above 300 AZN and up to 2,000 AZN requires the written approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee is also the department manager and provides the written approval, because the policy does not forbid the claimant from being the approver.
findings.fix: Add a clause: “The approving department manager must be a different employee than the claimant.”
findings.reason: The policy does not forbid the claimant from also being the approving department manager.

findings.policy_basis: An employee may request a cash advance of up to 1,000 AZN for a business trip.
findings.scenario: The employee requests a 1,000 AZN advance for a short trip, then later requests an additional advance for the same trip, exploiting the absence of a rule that forbids multiple advances for one trip.
findings.fix: Add a rule stating that only one cash advance may be requested per business trip.
findings.reason: The policy permits a cash advance up to 1,000 AZN but does not limit the number of advances per trip, allowing multiple advances for the same trip.

findings.policy_basis: Client entertainment is reimbursed up to 100 AZN per person, with the approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee records entertainment for ten different “clients” (using generic names) in a single claim, each at the 100 AZN limit, exploiting the lack of a total cap on the number of persons.
findings.fix: Introduce a total maximum amount or limit on the number of client‑entertainment reimbursements per claim/trip.
findings.reason: There is no overall cap on the number of clients reimbursed, so an employee can claim the maximum 100 AZN for each of many clients.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense of up to 300 AZN may be approved by the employee's line supervisor.
findings.scenario: The employee submits three separate expense items of 300 AZN each for the same business purpose; each item is approved by the line supervisor, allowing a total reimbursement of 900 AZN despite the rule applying only to a single expense.
findings.fix: Add: "An employee may not submit more than one expense item for the same business purpose within a single reimbursement period."
findings.reason: The rule limits a single expense but does not limit the number of separate expenses for the same purpose, allowing multiple 300 AZN items to be approved.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
findings.scenario: The employee reports a travel period of fifteen days, even though the trip only lasted three days, and receives 60 AZN for every reported day because the rule does not restrict how many days may be claimed.
findings.fix: Per‑diem may be claimed only for actual travel days, verified by a travel itinerary or approved travel order.
findings.reason: The per‑diem rule sets a daily amount but imposes no limit on the number of days that can be claimed.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
findings.scenario: The employee submits two separate travel requests for the same calendar week, each with a per‑diem claim, effectively doubling the 60 AZN per day because the policy does not forbid overlapping claims.
findings.fix: Overlapping travel requests for the same period shall be rejected and per‑diem may be claimed only once per calendar day.
findings.reason: The policy does not forbid submitting overlapping travel requests, enabling double‑paying the per‑diem for the same days.

findings.policy_basis: The same expense may not be claimed more than once.
findings.scenario: The employee divides a hotel stay of 3 nights (total 450 AZN) into three separate nightly claims, each treated as a distinct expense, thereby bypassing the single‑expense prohibition.
findings.fix: Define a “single expense” as any cost for the same service incurred on the same trip and prohibit splitting it into multiple claims.
findings.reason: The policy forbids claiming the same expense more than once but does not define a “single expense,” so splitting a hotel stay into separate nightly claims evades the restriction.

findings.policy_basis: The department manager decides whether a trip is necessary.
findings.scenario: Because the policy does not forbid the department manager from being the claimant, an employee who also holds the department‑manager role can unilaterally decide that their own trip is necessary.
findings.fix: The department manager may not be the claimant for a trip they approve; approval must come from a higher‑level manager.
findings.reason: The policy does not forbid the department manager from being the claimant, so a manager can self‑approve their own trip.

findings.policy_basis: Air travel must be booked in economy class.
findings.scenario: The employee purchases a first‑class ticket and claims reimbursement for the same amount, arguing that the policy only states a requirement, not a penalty for non‑compliance.
findings.fix: Any air‑travel expense exceeding the economy‑class fare must be approved in writing by the Finance Director and will be reimbursed only up to the economy fare.
findings.reason: The policy only states a requirement but provides no enforcement, so a first‑class ticket can be reimbursed without consequence.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense of up to 300 AZN may be approved by the employee's line supervisor.
findings.scenario: The employee is also the line supervisor and approves his own hotel claim (each night is a separate expense of 150 AZN, all under the 300 AZN approval limit).
findings.fix: Expenses may only be approved by a supervisor who is not the claimant.
findings.reason: The rule permits a supervisor to approve expenses up to 300 AZN and does not require the approver to be a different person.

findings.policy_basis: An employee may request a cash advance of up to 1,000 AZN for a business trip.
findings.scenario: The employee requests a 1,000 AZN advance even though no business trip has been approved yet, because the rule does not require prior travel authorization before the advance request.
findings.fix: Require that a travel request be approved before any cash advance may be issued.
findings.reason: The rule allows a cash advance without requiring prior travel authorization.

findings.policy_basis: The advance must be settled after the trip by submitting receipts or returning the unspent cash.
findings.scenario: The employee never returns the unspent cash nor submits receipts, and the policy provides no deadline or penalty for failing to settle the advance, allowing the amount to remain unaccounted.
findings.fix: Mandate that advances be settled within 30 days of trip completion, with penalties for non‑settlement.
findings.reason: The policy does not set a deadline or penalty for settling an advance, allowing it to remain unaccounted.

findings.policy_basis: No receipts are required for the per diem.
findings.scenario: The employee submits per‑diem claims for ten separate travel days without any supporting documentation, relying on the explicit exemption from receipt requirements.
findings.fix: Per diem claims must be supported by a signed travel itinerary and a statement confirming that no other meal reimbursements were received.
findings.reason: The rule explicitly states no receipts are required for per diem, allowing unlimited undocumented claims.

findings.policy_basis: The advance must be settled after the trip by submitting receipts or returning the unspent cash.
findings.scenario: The employee returns only a portion of the unspent cash and keeps the remainder, arguing that the rule allows settlement by “returning the unspent cash” without specifying that the full amount must be returned.
findings.fix: Specify that any unspent portion of a cash advance must be returned in full before reimbursement is processed.
findings.reason: The wording allows returning “the unspent cash” without stating it must be the full amount, enabling partial retention.

findings.policy_basis: Late claims may be accepted with the consent of the department manager.
findings.scenario: Because there is no cap on the number of late claims, the employee repeatedly submits small late expenses (each under 50 AZN) with the same informal consent, accumulating a large total reimbursement.
findings.fix: Introduce a maximum total amount or number of late‑claim submissions per employee per fiscal year.
findings.reason: No limit on the number or total amount of late claims lets an employee accumulate large reimbursements.

findings.policy_basis: A single expense of up to 300 AZN may be approved by the employee's line supervisor.
findings.scenario: The employee is also the line supervisor for their own position and signs the approval for a 300 AZN expense, satisfying the rule because the policy does not prohibit the claimant from being the approver.
findings.fix: Add: "The approving supervisor must be a different employee than the claimant."
findings.reason: The policy does not require the approver to be a different person, so a claimant can approve their own 300 AZN expense.

findings.policy_basis: Hotel accommodation is reimbursed up to 150 AZN per night.
findings.scenario: The employee books two separate rooms for the same night, each costing 150 AZN, and submits two separate claims, since the rule does not restrict the number of rooms or require a single‑room limit.
findings.fix: Specify that only one room per night may be reimbursed unless a separate business justification is provided.
findings.reason: The rule permits 150 AZN per night but does not restrict the number of rooms that can be claimed for the same night.

findings.policy_basis: An original receipt or invoice must be attached to every expense claim above 50 AZN.
findings.scenario: The employee divides a 200 AZN hotel bill into four separate entries of 50 AZN each; no receipt is required for any entry, so the full amount is reimbursed without supporting documents.
findings.fix: Add: "The total amount of related expenses for a single vendor or stay must be aggregated for receipt‑attachment purposes."
findings.reason: Dividing a 200 AZN hotel bill into four 50 AZN entries avoids the receipt requirement, even though the total expense exceeds the threshold.

findings.policy_basis: The employee must record the names of the clients entertained.
findings.scenario: The employee records the same client name repeatedly for multiple entertainment events, because the rule does not limit how many times a single client may appear.
findings.fix: Add a limit on the number of entertainment reimbursements per client within a given period.
findings.reason: The policy does not limit how many times the same client can appear, allowing repeated reimbursements for a single client.

findings.policy_basis: Finance Department ... may update it at any time.
findings.scenario: The employee submits a claim under the current 150 AZN hotel limit, and after approval the Finance Department lowers the limit to 100 AZN; the claim remains payable because the policy does not state that updates apply retroactively.
findings.fix: All policy updates shall apply to pending and future expense claims; any claim approved under a previous limit must be adjusted to the current limit before payment.
findings.reason: The policy allows the Finance Department to update the rules at any time but does not state that updates apply retroactively, so a claim approved under the old 150 AZN hotel limit can remain payable after the limit is lowered.

findings.policy_basis: Client entertainment is reimbursed up to 100 AZN per person, with the approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The department manager, who is also the employee requesting reimbursement, signs off on the entertainment claim, because the policy does not state that the approver must be different from the claimant.
findings.fix: Specify that the approving department manager must be a different individual than the employee submitting the claim.
findings.reason: The policy requires department‑manager approval but does not require the approver to be a different person from the claimant.

findings.policy_basis: Client entertainment is reimbursed up to 100 AZN per person, with the approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee records a fictitious client name and claims 100 AZN for that “person,” exploiting the lack of any verification requirement for the client‑name list.
findings.fix: Mandate that client names be verified against an approved client list or require supporting documentation of the entertainment.
findings.reason: No verification of client names is required, so fictitious clients can be recorded to obtain the full per‑person reimbursement.

findings.policy_basis: The employee must record the names of the clients entertained.
findings.scenario: The employee lists fictitious client names for each entertainment entry, satisfying the recording requirement while creating reimbursements for non‑existent clients.
findings.fix: Require that client names be verifiable (e.g., by providing a client contract or contact confirmation).
findings.reason: The rule only requires that client names be recorded; it does not require verification of their existence.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs. No receipts are required for the per diem.
findings.scenario: The employee includes alcoholic drinks in the per‑diem claim, relying on the “no receipts” clause, while the explicit ban on alcohol does not apply to per‑diem amounts.
findings.fix: Add a clause: “The per‑diem may not be used to reimburse alcoholic beverages.”
findings.reason: The ban on alcohol does not explicitly apply to per‑diem amounts, which have no receipt requirement.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
findings.scenario: The employee labels weekend days before the official travel start and after the travel end as “travel days” and claims the 60 AZN per diem for those days, because the rule does not define when a travel day begins or ends.
findings.fix: Define a travel day as any day on which the employee is officially on business travel, i.e., between the approved departure and return dates.
findings.reason: The per‑diem rule lacks a definition of when a travel day starts and ends, enabling claims for non‑travel days.

findings.policy_basis: The advance must be settled after the trip by submitting receipts or returning the unspent cash.
findings.scenario: After using the cash advance for personal items under 50 AZN (which do not require receipts per Article 3.1), the employee returns the remaining cash and submits only the required receipts, effectively keeping the unrecorded personal spend.
findings.fix: Require that all expenditures from a cash advance be supported by receipts, regardless of amount, or that the full amount be returned if not documented.
findings.reason: Receipts are only required for expenses above 50 AZN, so personal purchases under that amount can be kept while the advance is settled with the required receipts.

findings.policy_basis: Expense claims must be submitted within 30 days.
findings.scenario: The employee submits the claim after 30 days but labels the claim as a “cash advance settlement,” exploiting the fact that the policy ties the deadline only to expense claims, not to advance reconciliations.
findings.fix: Require that cash‑advance settlements be submitted within the same 30‑day period as expense claims.
findings.reason: The policy sets a 30‑day limit only for expense claims and does not bind cash‑advance settlements, allowing late settlement to bypass the deadline.

findings.policy_basis: Late claims may be accepted with the consent of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee, who is also the department manager, gives consent to his own late claim, because the policy does not require the consentor to be a different person.
findings.fix: Specify that consent for late claims must be provided by a manager other than the employee submitting the claim.
findings.reason: Consent for late claims may be given by the department manager, and the rule does not require the consentor to be a different person.

findings.policy_basis: Domestic business travel is permitted when it is necessary.
findings.scenario: The employee argues that attending a personal conference is “necessary” for networking, and because the policy does not require any evidence of necessity, the travel is approved.
findings.fix: Domestic business travel is permitted only when it is necessary and the necessity must be documented in writing and approved by the department manager.
findings.reason: The rule allows travel when "necessary" but does not require any proof, so an employee can claim any trip is necessary and obtain approval.

findings.policy_basis: Domestic business travel is permitted when it is necessary.
findings.scenario: The policy does not tie the necessity determination to any written approval; the employee obtains a casual verbal affirmation from the department manager and proceeds with travel.
findings.fix: The department manager's decision on travel necessity must be recorded in writing and retained with the expense claim.
findings.reason: The policy does not specify the form of the manager's decision, allowing a casual verbal affirmation to satisfy the requirement.

findings.policy_basis: The department manager decides whether a trip is necessary.
findings.scenario: The policy does not require the decision to be recorded, so the employee obtains an informal “okay” from the department manager via a quick chat message and treats the trip as authorized.
findings.fix: The decision of the department manager on travel necessity must be documented in a formal written approval stored in the expense system.
findings.reason: Because the rule does not require the decision to be recorded, an informal chat message suffices as authorization.

findings.policy_basis: Air travel must be booked in economy class.
findings.scenario: The employee books a business‑class ticket but records the fare as “economy” on the claim; the policy provides no verification mechanism, so the claim is accepted.
findings.fix: Air travel tickets must be accompanied by a class‑verification document; reimbursement will be limited to the economy‑class fare.
findings.reason: The economy‑class requirement lacks any verification or penalty, allowing a higher‑class ticket to be claimed as economy.

findings.policy_basis: Client entertainment is reimbursed up to 100 AZN per person, with the approval of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee obtains a written approval from a different department manager who has no oversight of the expense, exploiting the rule’s silence on who must give the approval.
findings.fix: State that approval for client‑entertainment expenses must be obtained from the employee’s direct department manager.
findings.reason: The rule only says “department manager” without specifying that it must be the manager of the employee’s own department.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
findings.scenario: The employee submits separate per‑diem claims for the same calendar day (e.g., morning and evening) each for 60 AZN, exploiting the absence of a rule that limits one per‑diem claim per day.
findings.fix: State that only one per‑diem payment of 60 AZN may be claimed for each travel day.
findings.reason: The policy does not limit the number of per‑diem claims per calendar day.

findings.policy_basis: A per diem of 60 AZN is paid for each day of travel to cover meals and incidental costs.
findings.scenario: The employee claims a per diem for a day on which all meals are provided by the client, because the policy does not require that meals be unpaid to qualify.
findings.fix: Per diem is payable only for days when the employee incurs meal expenses not covered by the client or host.
findings.reason: The rule does not require that meals be unpaid, so per‑diem can be claimed even when meals are provided.

findings.policy_basis: No receipts are required for the per diem.
findings.scenario: The employee files per‑diem claims for days that were only partially spent on business (e.g., a half‑day conference), because the rule does not define what constitutes a “day of travel.”
findings.fix: Define a “day of travel” as a full business day on which the employee is engaged in work‑related activities for at least 4 hours.
findings.reason: The rule omits a definition of “day of travel,” allowing claims for partial‑day trips to be treated as full days.

findings.policy_basis: An original receipt or invoice must be attached to every expense claim above 50 AZN.
findings.scenario: The employee reports a single 55 AZN expense but claims it is a “cash advance settlement” and therefore submits the advance voucher instead of the original receipt, because the policy does not require a receipt for advances.
findings.fix: Add a clause: “All expense claims, including cash‑advance settlements, must include the original receipt for amounts above 50 AZN.”
findings.reason: A cash‑advance settlement is treated as exempt from the receipt rule, allowing a 55 AZN expense without a receipt.

findings.policy_basis: An original receipt or invoice must be attached to every expense claim above 50 AZN.
findings.scenario: Because the policy does not define what constitutes an “original” receipt, the employee submits a photocopy of a receipt and claims it satisfies the requirement.
findings.fix: Specify that an original receipt must be the vendor‑issued document, not a copy or scan.
findings.reason: “Original receipt” is undefined, so a photocopy can be used.

findings.policy_basis: Expense claims must be submitted within 30 days.
findings.scenario: The policy does not define from which date the 30‑day period is measured; the employee submits a claim 35 days after the travel end date but 20 days after the date the receipt was issued, arguing compliance with the unspecified reference point.
findings.fix: Add: "The 30‑day submission deadline is calculated from the date the expense was incurred or the travel end date, whichever is later."
findings.reason: The policy does not specify whether the 30‑day deadline is measured from the travel end date or receipt date, allowing a claim to be submitted after the travel period but within 30 days of receipt issuance.

findings.policy_basis: Expense claims must be submitted within 30 days.
findings.scenario: The employee submits a claim on day 31 but includes a note that the claim was prepared on day 30, exploiting the lack of a required timestamp or verification of the submission date.
findings.fix: Expense claims must include a system‑generated timestamp proving submission within 30 days of the expense date.
findings.reason: The policy lacks a required timestamp or verification of the submission date, allowing a claim submitted after 30 days to be accepted by claiming it was prepared earlier.

findings.policy_basis: Expense claims must be submitted within 30 days.
findings.scenario: The policy does not state any consequence for exceeding the 30‑day limit, so the employee submits a claim on day 45 without any manager consent and the claim is still processed.
findings.fix: State that claims submitted after 30 days will be rejected unless written manager consent is provided.
findings.reason: No penalty is stated for exceeding the 30‑day deadline, so late claims can be processed.

findings.policy_basis: Late claims may be accepted with the consent of the department manager.
findings.scenario: The employee obtains a verbal email from the department manager stating “you may submit late,” exploiting the lack of any formal format or documentation requirement for the consent.
findings.fix: Require written, signed consent on a designated form for any late claim approval.
findings.reason: The rule allows late claims with department‑manager consent but does not mandate any particular form or documentation of that consent.

findings.policy_basis: Domestic business travel is permitted when it is necessary.
findings.scenario: The employee schedules a weekend trip to a client’s office, arguing that the weekend travel is still “necessary,” and the policy provides no restriction on days of the week.
findings.fix: Domestic business travel may be reimbursed only for trips occurring on regular business days unless a specific business need for weekend travel is documented and approved.
findings.reason: The policy does not restrict travel to weekdays, allowing weekend trips to be claimed as “necessary.”

findings.policy_basis: Domestic business travel is permitted when it is necessary.
findings.scenario: The employee schedules a short 2‑hour trip and claims it as business travel, because the policy does not set a minimum distance or duration for “travel.”
findings.fix: Introduce a minimum distance or duration threshold for travel to be eligible for reimbursement.
findings.reason: The policy does not set a minimum distance or duration for travel, so a short 2‑hour trip can be claimed as business travel.

findings.policy_basis: The department manager decides whether a trip is necessary.
findings.scenario: A colleague with the title of department manager signs off on the employee’s travel request, even though the manager has no direct oversight of that employee, exploiting the absence of a rule linking managerial responsibility to the decision.
findings.fix: Only the direct department manager of the employee may decide whether a trip is necessary.
findings.reason: The policy does not require the approving department manager to have direct oversight of the employee, permitting unrelated managers to approve travel.

findings.policy_basis: The employee must record the names of the clients entertained.
findings.scenario: The employee lists generic placeholders (e.g., “Client A”) without confirming actual attendance, because the rule only mandates recording names and does not require proof of the entertainment.
findings.fix: Require that recorded client names be accompanied by evidence of the entertainment (e.g., receipts, sign‑in sheet).
findings.reason: The rule only demands recording names, not proof of actual attendance, permitting placeholder entries.
